idiom_name: one facade type per cohesive abstraction, owning the handle
implementation_notes: Pick the cohesive abstractions hidden in the loose API (one per resource kind: lock, thread, socket, file, session, codec) and define one facade type per abstraction whose methods coalesce the raw calls into intent-named operations and hide the handle. Acquire in the constructor/factory and release in the destructor, close() or scope-exit hook, so callers cannot forget teardown without a visible mistake. Keep the published interface platform-independent and put the per-platform differences either in conditional method bodies or in per-platform implementations selected at build time. Forward directly unless a second implementation genuinely exists; when it does, make the facade the abstraction of a Bridge and delegate to an implementation object. Expose the raw handle only through a deliberate, documented escape hatch, and translate errors at the boundary while preserving the original code.
code_sketch:
class Mutex:                                  # one facade per cohesive abstraction
    def __init__(self): self._h = raw_init()   # acquire in the constructor
    def acquire(self): check_ok(raw_lock(self._h))   # coalesce + translate errors
    def release(self): check_ok(raw_unlock(self._h))
    def close(self):   raw_destroy(self._h)    # single teardown path
# call sites never see the handle, the raw functions, or their error convention
pitfalls: A facade that only renames functions: no coalescing, no ownership, no portability - the abstraction has to earn its extra layer.
Handing the raw handle to callers or to other components, which then bypass the facade's invariants and invalidate its lifetime rules.
One facade instance shared by concurrent callers when the underlying handle is not thread-safe: state the thread-safety contract or let the facade own the lock.

Wrong move: relying on the finalizer or destructor alone for teardown -> in garbage-collected languages release happens at an unpredictable time (and native teardown can throw or block in a destructor), so sockets pile up and shutdown order inverts -> expose an explicit close()/Dispose() that is idempotent and thread-safe, with the finalizer only as a backstop (.NET SafeHandle pairs Close/Dispose with a critical finalizer for exactly this reason).

Wrong move: translating every native failure into one generic error or a best-effort default return -> callers can no longer distinguish retryable conditions like EAGAIN, WSAETIMEDOUT or a transient driver busy-code and either retry the unretryable or give up too early -> raise a typed facade error that carries the original errno/HRESULT so the call site can still branch on the real condition.

Wrong move: wrapping a borrowed native handle with the same wrapper type used for owned ones -> the destructor closes a handle someone else still owns, producing double-close or use-after-free that surfaces far from the fault -> separate ownership at the type level (OwnedFd vs BorrowedFd in Rust, ownsHandle=false in SafeHandle) or give borrowed wraps a non-closing type.
